source.title: Resurrecting the Salmon: Rethinking Mechanistic Interpretability with Domain-Specific Sparse Autoencoders
source.authors: Charles O'Neill; M. Jayasekara; Max Kirkby

record.tranche_reason: Measures SAE error predictability using the dark-matter framework and compares it across domain-specific and broad-domain SAEs, but uses a different model/data/training setup rather than reproducing the original study.
record.gate_note: The dark-matter results report trends across widths and sparsities, but Figure 5 does not provide values that can be reliably assigned to each individual configuration from the supplied text. Loss-recovery results do not compare SAE errors with random errors of the same size, and the steering statements do not test whether retaining the error term preserves behaviour; these are not rows for V3 or V5.
record.test_reason: Applies the three dark-matter measures of Engels et al. to GemmaScope and new medical-domain JumpReLU SAEs at layer 20 of Gemma-2-9b. These are error-norm R², error-vector R² and nonlinear FVU. The new setting is domain-confined SAEs, evaluated on medical text. The results bear on V1, V2 (norm-predictability part) and V4.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that domain-confined SAEs capture most of the linear structure, leaving a smaller, more nonlinear residual, and that domain-specific training should replace broad 'foundation' SAE scaling. The record should note that their own Fig. 5 still shows error-vector R² of about 0.56–0.73 for the domain SAEs.
record.recipe_differences: Uses linear prediction of error norm and full error vector, and a nonlinear residual measure inspired by Engels et al. (2024), but compares medical-domain JumpReLU SAEs with GemmaScope SAEs on Gemma-2-9b rather than reproducing the original study’s setup.
record.method_sensitivity: Training domain changes the reported residual predictability: domain-specific versus broad-domain SAE. Width and sparsity are swept, with trends described as consistent across tested settings.

fits_no_version.finding: Medical-domain SAEs show lower error-vector and error-norm linear predictability than GemmaScope SAEs of the same widths.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Restricting SAE training data to a narrow domain reduces the linearly predictable part of SAE error on that domain.

fits_no_version.finding: Domain SAEs explain about 15–20% more variance and recover more loss than GemmaScope SAEs (Figs 2–3).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Domain-specific SAEs reconstruct in-domain activations more faithfully than broad SAEs.

fits_no_version.finding: The authors assert more precise steering, with no results shown.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Domain-specific SAE features give more targeted steering.

record.problems: The dark-matter results are presented as plots without reliably attributable numerical values for individual widths and sparsities in the supplied text. The study does not test token-level error overlap across SAE sizes or compare SAE reconstruction errors with random errors of matched size. The full model training and domain comparison are limited to the stated Gemma-2 setup and medical-text corpus.
record.rows_left_out: No per-width or per-sparsity rows were extracted from Figure 5 because the supplied text does not permit reliable assignment of its plotted values to individual configurations; the aggregate trends explicitly described in Section 4.3 are recorded instead. Loss-recovery and steering statements are not rows because they do not test the measures specified by V3 or V5.

untested.parts: Same-context failure across SAE sizes; whether error persists as width grows. Fig. 5 shows only 16k and 32k, with no per-width trend reported.
No comparison of SAE-error loss against norm-matched random errors. Loss recovered is reported only.
No direct test that the linear part consists of unlearned features, or that larger or extra dictionaries fail on the nonlinear part.
No circuit or steering analysis with versus without the error term. Steering is only asserted.
Sparsity penalty, dead latents, objective, architecture and end-to-end training are not varied. Only the training data domain changes.

missing.what: Relative reconstruction bias is about 1 for both SAE families (minimal shrinkage), yet dark matter remains. This bears on the shrinkage part of V6.
Numeric ranges for the Fig. 5 metrics are readable from the colourbars and should replace 'figure only' in R1–R6.

record.verdict_notes: The V6 links are removed because changing the training corpus is a capacity-allocation or data choice, not the SAE training artifacts V6 names. The dataset used for the dark-matter evaluation is not stated, presumably medical text. Fig. 5 covers only widths 16k and 32k, although SAEs up to 2^20 were trained. No uncertainty is reported. The authors' wording 'not substantially inflated' understates the remaining linear predictability.

versions.untested_parts: Does not establish a numerical ‘large share’ threshold; the text describes relative predictability rather than reporting attributable per-configuration values.

Tests prediction of squared error norm from the input over SAE widths, but does not test cross-size predictability of the same tokens, whether larger SAEs fail on the same contexts, or whether error fails to vanish with scale.
Does not compare reconstruction-induced loss with random errors of the same size.
Does not directly establish that the linear component consists of specific features not yet learned, or test whether further dictionary learning fails to capture the nonlinear component.
Does not measure behaviour or circuit/steering performance with versus without the SAE error term.

Tests domain-specific versus broad-domain SAE training, but not sparsity penalties, shrinkage, dead latents, alternative objectives, improved architectures, or end-to-end training; it does not establish that training accounts for most dark matter.
